title: The Realities of Teaching 40–75 Students
brief: Open by naming the core problems the source identifies for large classes: insufficient planning time, difficulty establishing rapport, limited monitoring and individual feedback, wide variation in proficiency that leaves weaker students behind, discipline challenges, and scarce opportunity for actual language production and practice. Explain that the source frames these not as reasons for despair but as a practical problem set that classroom management skills and a focused list of pedagogical techniques can address. Draw directly on the Module 6 Introduction's bulleted problem list and its statement that effective learning in large classes depends more on management skills and a short list of pedagogical techniques than on any single teaching approach.

title: Pedagogical Planning: Knowing Your Students and Setting Goals
brief: Cover the source's pedagogical planning techniques: giving diagnostic tests at the start of term to discover each student's strengths and needs; helping students set their own learning goals and develop personal learning strategies; thinking of students as 'works in progress' with a range of abilities rather than labelling them; and learning student names or using identifiers such as name cards so students feel known and important. Also include the source's rotation strategy—creating a plan that gives individual attention to a particular set of students each day so that over two to three days every student or group receives some individual attention. Draw exclusively on the Video Segment 1 Answer Key narrative.

title: Classroom Learning Systems: Routines That Scale
brief: Explain what the source means by 'classroom learning systems'—clear routines, expectations, and physical arrangements that save time, help learners know what is expected, and add to their sense of security. Cover the specific teacher routines listed in the Video Segment 2 Answer Key: posting the day's agenda on the board, setting up routines for attendance, homework correction, paper distribution and collection, keeping explanations and directions clear and brief, and having additional self-directed activities ready for students who finish early. Include the source's note on physical organisation—desks grouped in clusters rather than rows, and learning stations used for different purposes—and the technique of calling on named table groups (larks, eagles, etc.) rather than releasing the whole class at once, as a concrete example of how routines manage movement efficiently.

title: Pair and Group Structures That Work at Scale
brief: Focus on the source's guidance for using pair and group structures in large classes. Draw on the Video Segment 2 Answer Key's student routines—moving smoothly from one activity to another, shifting in and out of group work quickly, and self-checking and peer-checking student work—to show how these structures distribute practice across the whole class simultaneously. Include the source's point about giving learners responsibility for choosing and doing individual projects within a group they have chosen, and displaying student work. Connect this to the source's broader principle of encouraging student responsibility and independence by allowing freedom within the established framework to make choices, help with classroom logistics, and help each other.

title: Monitoring and Feedback When You Cannot Reach Everyone
brief: Address the monitoring challenge directly using the source's solutions. Explain the rotation system from Video Segment 1—planning to give individual attention to a different set of students each day so that every student receives attention over a two-to-three-day cycle. Add the Video Segment 2 Answer Key's point that teachers individualise feedback by checking in with different pairs and small groups as they circulate. Include the source's suggestion to use any available aides or volunteer help effectively as an additional monitoring resource. Tie these techniques back to the source's identified problem: that in large classes learners may get little individual attention or feedback to help them improve, making systematic rotation and targeted circulation essential rather than optional.

title: Keeping Weaker Students Engaged: Discipline and Inclusion
brief: Cover the source's discipline management framework and its role in keeping all students, including weaker ones, engaged. Explain the source's proactive versus reactive distinction: establishing clear rules and expectations before problems arise, posting rules in both the first and second language, and letting students help create agreed-on classroom conduct guides. Include the source's points on consistency—applying rules the same way for all students at all times—using reward systems and peer reinforcement so the whole class works toward shared behavioural goals, and postponing individual discipline matters until after class to protect learning time. Add the source's guidance on building purposeful activities and opportunities for movement into lesson plans, and on trying to discover the reasons behind persistent negative behaviour rather than simply reacting to it. Note the source's statement that humiliating students makes it difficult for them to learn or want to learn, and that respecting students encourages them to respect the teacher in return.
